subject: food-technology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does the term 'food provenance' mean?
options: Where food comes from and how it is produced
The number of calories in a food
The way food is cooked at home
The price a shop charges for food
questions.explain: Food provenance is about the origin of food and the methods used to produce, grow, rear or catch it.

questions.q: What is meant by the term 'food miles'?
options: The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten
The weight of food a lorry can carry
The number of shops that sell a food
The shelf life of a food in days
questions.explain: Food miles measure the distance food is transported, which affects its environmental impact.

questions.q: Which logo shows that producers in developing countries have received a fair, guaranteed price?
options: Fairtrade
Red Tractor
Freezer Star
The Lion Mark
questions.explain: The Fairtrade mark guarantees producers a fair and stable price for their goods.

questions.q: Which certification scheme indicates fish that has been caught from a sustainable source?
options: MSC (Marine Stewardship Council)
RSPCA Assured
Soil Association
Vegetarian Society
questions.explain: The MSC label shows fish has been caught using sustainable methods that protect fish stocks.

questions.q: What is meant by 'seasonal food'?
options: Food that is naturally grown and harvested at a particular time of the year
Food that can only be bought at Christmas
Food that has been frozen for later use
Food that is imported from other countries
questions.explain: Seasonal foods are grown and harvested during their natural growing season in a particular region.

questions.q: How is organic food produced?
options: Without artificial pesticides, herbicides or fertilisers
Using extra artificial chemicals to speed up growth
Only in a laboratory from synthetic ingredients
Always by genetically modifying the crop
questions.explain: Organic farming avoids artificial chemicals and follows strict welfare and environmental standards.

questions.q: What does the term 'free-range' most accurately describe?
options: Animals that have access to the outdoors and space to roam
Animals kept permanently indoors in cages
Food produced without any packaging
Food sold at a reduced price
questions.explain: Free-range animals are given outdoor access and more space, improving their welfare.

questions.q: What is a 'carbon footprint'?
options: The total amount of greenhouse gases produced by an activity or product
The amount of water used to grow a crop
The weight of packaging on a product
The number of food miles a product travels
questions.explain: A carbon footprint measures the greenhouse gas emissions linked to producing, transporting and using a product.

questions.q: Why does buying locally produced food generally benefit the environment?
options: It reduces food miles and the emissions from transporting food
It always makes the food cheaper to buy
It removes the need for any farming
It increases the amount of packaging used
questions.explain: Local food travels shorter distances, lowering transport emissions and its carbon footprint.

questions.q: Which piece of information on a food label tells you where a product was produced?
options: Country of origin
Best before date
Bar code
Net weight
questions.explain: The country of origin shows consumers where the food was grown, reared or caught.

questions.q: What is genetically modified (GM) food?
options: Food whose genetic material has been altered to give it desirable characteristics
Food that has been frozen and defrosted
Food grown only using organic methods
Food that has passed its use-by date
questions.explain: GM food has had its DNA changed, for example to resist pests or improve yield.

questions.q: Why is excessive food packaging a concern for the environment?
options: It creates waste and can contribute to landfill and pollution
It always makes food less nutritious
It reduces the number of food miles
It guarantees food is organic
questions.explain: Unnecessary packaging uses resources and adds to waste and pollution unless it is recycled or reduced.

questions.q: What is the best description of 'sustainable food production'?
options: Producing food to meet present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
Producing as much food as possible regardless of impact
Only producing food in greenhouses
Producing food using the cheapest methods available
questions.explain: Sustainability means using resources responsibly so food can continue to be produced in the future.

questions.q: What does 'food security' mean?
options: People having reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food
Keeping food locked in a secure warehouse
Food that is high in preservatives
Food that is only sold in supermarkets
questions.explain: Food security means everyone has consistent access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food.

questions.q: How does transporting food long distances by air affect the environment?
options: It increases greenhouse gas emissions and the carbon footprint
It reduces the food's food miles
It has no effect on the environment
It makes the food organic
questions.explain: Air freight produces high emissions, increasing the food's carbon footprint and food miles.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of primary processing?
options: Milling wheat grains into flour
Baking flour into a cake
Frying potatoes into crisps
Turning milk into cheese
questions.explain: Primary processing is the first stage that turns a raw ingredient into a usable form, such as milling wheat into flour.

questions.q: A family wants to reduce the carbon footprint of their weekly shop. Which choice would best help?
options: Buying local, seasonal fruit and vegetables
Buying air-freighted fruit out of season
Choosing items with the most packaging
Buying food from the furthest possible source
questions.explain: Local, seasonal produce has fewer food miles and lower emissions, reducing the shop's carbon footprint.

questions.q: A school canteen wants to be more sustainable. Which action best reduces food waste?
options: Planning menus carefully and composting unavoidable food scraps
Cooking far more food than needed each day
Throwing all leftovers straight into landfill
Using extra individually wrapped portions
questions.explain: Good planning cuts waste, and composting scraps keeps unavoidable waste out of landfill.

questions.q: In summer in the UK, which of these is most likely to be in season and locally grown?
options: Strawberries
Mangoes
Pineapples
Bananas
questions.explain: Strawberries are grown and harvested in the UK during the summer, unlike tropical imported fruits.

questions.q: A shopper chooses a bar of chocolate carrying the Fairtrade mark. What is the main benefit of this choice?
options: Producers in developing countries receive a fair and stable price for their crop
The chocolate contains fewer calories
The chocolate has travelled fewer food miles
The chocolate is guaranteed to be organic
questions.explain: Choosing Fairtrade helps ensure growers are paid fairly, supporting more sustainable livelihoods.
